keyVerseText: And his concubine, whose name was Reumah, she bare also Tebah, and Gaham, and Thahash, and Maachah.
rootMeaning: The root of רְאוּמָה (Reumah) is רָאַם (râʼam), which means "to be lifted up" or "to rise." As a feminine passive participle, רְאוּמָה conveys the sense of being "elevated" or "raised." This etymology enriches the understanding of the name beyond a simple proper noun, suggesting a status of elevation or honor that may reflect the character or position of the individual named.
usageInScripture: The word רְאוּמָה appears only once in Scripture, specifically in Genesis 22:24, where it is used as the proper name of Nahor's concubine. The sole translation recorded is "was Reumah," indicating that it is consistently treated as a proper name without variation. This singular usage highlights the personal identity of Reumah within the narrative, rather than functioning as a descriptive term.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding רְאוּמָה as "elevated" invites reflection on how God raises individuals in His providence, even those who may seem peripheral in the biblical story. Reumah, though a concubine, is named and thus given significance, reminding believers that God values all persons and their roles in His unfolding plan. This elevation can also point to the broader biblical theme of God lifting up the lowly, which finds its ultimate fulfillment in Christ. Recognizing the root meaning deepens appreciation for the personal histories woven into Scripture and God's sovereign care over every life.
keyVerseReflection: Genesis 22:24 introduces Reumah as Nahor's concubine and mother of several sons, emphasizing her role in the family lineage. The use of her name, meaning "elevated," subtly honors her position within this household. This detail enriches the verse by highlighting that even those not primary wives hold an important place in God's covenant community, contributing to the unfolding narrative of His promises.
